title: System Design Fundamentals: Scale, Caching and Load Balancing
subtitle: Design systems that scale: estimate the load, then choose load balancers, caches, databases and queues, and defend every trade-off.
outcomes: Turn an open-ended brief into measurable requirements, an API and back-of-the-envelope estimates
Reason about latency with orders of magnitude, percentiles and Little's law
Choose load-balancing, rate-limiting, caching and CDN strategies, and explain how each one fails
Scale a database with indexes, read replicas and shards placed by consistent hashing
Make retries and redeliveries safe with idempotency keys, deduplicating consumers and the outbox pattern
Build and test a token-bucket limiter, an LRU cache and a consistent-hash ring in Python
prerequisites: Confident Python (functions, classes, dictionaries) and basic SQL: Python Programming with PyCharm and SQL for Data Analysis with DataGrip cover them, and Networking Fundamentals: How Networks and the Internet Work helps with HTTP and DNS. Install Python 3.10 or newer and pytest (python -m pip install pytest). Redis and curl are needed only for three walkthroughs.
description:
System design is the craft of turning a product idea into services, stores and queues that stay fast and correct as traffic grows. This course teaches it the way experienced engineers practise it: pin down the requirements, estimate the load with round numbers, sketch the simplest design that meets them, then go deep on the parts that will break first. You'll learn how load balancers spread traffic and how rate limits, timeouts and circuit breakers stop one failure becoming an outage; how caches and CDNs keep reads fast, and how they go stale; how replication and sharding scale a database; and how queues and idempotency keys make asynchronous work and retries safe. Worked designs of a URL shortener, a chat service and a news feed show the pieces working together.

The labs make the building blocks concrete: you'll write a capacity calculator, a token-bucket rate limiter, an LRU cache with TTLs, a consistent-hash ring and an idempotent payment API in Python, each with pytest tests and a simulation whose output you can check. The capstone asks you to design a live delivery-tracking service and prototype its core from those pieces. Afterwards, Distributed Systems: Replication, Consensus and Consistency goes deeper into replicated stores, Database Internals: Indexes, Transactions and Query Plans goes inside a single database, and Foundations of AI System Design applies the same thinking to machine learning systems.

modules.title: Requirements, estimates and latency
modules.summary: Start every design the same way: pin down what the system must do and how well, estimate its traffic, storage and bandwidth with round numbers, and know each building block's latency to within an order of magnitude.

lessons.title: From a vague brief to requirements
objectives: Separate functional from non-functional requirements in a design brief
State non-functional requirements as measurable targets
Work through a design in a repeatable order, from requirements to deep dives
key_points: Functional requirements say what the system does (shorten a URL, redirect a short link, report clicks); non-functional requirements say how well: availability, latency, throughput, durability, consistency and cost. Most design decisions are driven by the non-functional ones.

Write non-functional requirements as numbers someone could test, such as '99.9% of redirects succeed each month' or 'p99 redirect latency under 100 ms', never 'fast and reliable'. Each number should change a decision, such as adding a cache or a replica.

Find out which operations dominate and how skewed the traffic is. A read-heavy system (many redirects per new link) favours caches and read replicas; a write-heavy one (chat messages, location updates) favours partitioned, append-friendly storage.

Say which data may be stale, and for how long: a bank balance must never be, a like count can lag by seconds. Data that tolerates staleness can be cached and replicated asynchronously; data that doesn't needs a single source of truth.
Agree the scope and write down what is out of it (custom domains, user accounts, an admin console), so the design time goes on the parts that matter.

Then work in a fixed order: the API (operations, inputs and outputs), the data model, a high-level diagram, and deep dives on the riskiest parts. Go back to the requirements whenever a deep dive changes an assumption.

lessons.title: Back-of-the-envelope estimates
objectives: Convert daily active users into average and peak requests per second
Estimate storage and bandwidth from object sizes, retention and copies
Translate an availability target into a downtime budget
key_points: A day has 86,400 seconds, roughly 10^5, so 1 million requests a day is about 12 a second on average. Multiply the average by a peak factor (often 2 to 10, depending on how bursty the traffic is) to size for the busiest period.
Use powers of two and ten together: 2^10 ≈ 10^3 (thousand, KB), 2^20 ≈ 10^6 (million, MB), 2^30 ≈ 10^9 (billion, GB) and 2^40 ≈ 10^12 (TB). So a billion 1 KB records is about 1 TB.
Storage = new objects per day × bytes per object × days retained × number of copies, plus room for indexes and growth. The aim is the right order of magnitude, not three significant figures.
Bandwidth = requests per second × bytes per response × 8 bits per byte. 1,000 requests a second of 500 KB images is 500 MB/s, or 4 Gbit/s, which points to a CDN rather than application servers.

Availability targets set a downtime budget: 99.9% allows about 8.8 hours a year (43 minutes a month) and 99.99% about 53 minutes a year. Parts in series multiply, so two 99.9% services that must both work give about 99.8%.
Write every assumption next to its estimate (users, actions per user, sizes, peak factor), so reviewers can challenge the inputs rather than redo the arithmetic.

lessons.title: Latency numbers and tail latency
objectives: Recall the latency of common operations to within an order of magnitude
Explain why percentiles, not averages, describe what users experience
Use Little's law to relate throughput, latency and concurrency
key_points: Orders of magnitude to know: a CPU cache hit about 1 ns, a main-memory read about 100 ns, a random SSD read tens to hundreds of microseconds, a round trip within a data centre roughly 0.1 to 0.5 ms, a spinning-disk seek around 10 ms, and a round trip between continents 100 ms or more.

The ratios matter more than the exact values: memory is hundreds to thousands of times faster than a random SSD read, and one cross-continent round trip costs as much as hundreds of calls inside a data centre. Hence caches in memory, and few sequential round trips between regions.

Describe latency with percentiles: p50 is the typical request and p99 the slowest 1%. An average hides the tail: a few very slow requests pull the mean well above the median while most users see neither.
Fan-out amplifies the tail: if a page waits for 100 back-end calls and each is slower than its p99 1% of the time, about 63% of page loads (1 − 0.99^100) include at least one slow call.

Little's law: the average number of requests in a system equals the arrival rate times the average time each spends there (L = λW). At 2,000 requests a second and 50 ms each, about 100 are in flight, which sizes thread and connection pools.
Hedged requests (send a second copy if the first hasn't answered by about the p95) and tight timeouts trim the tail at the cost of extra load; use them only for idempotent reads.

modules.title: Load balancing, rate limiting and resilience
modules.summary: Scale out behind load balancers, protect services with rate limits, and keep one slow dependency from taking everything down with timeouts, careful retries and circuit breakers.

lessons.title: Scaling out: stateless services and load balancers
objectives: Compare vertical and horizontal scaling
Explain what makes a service stateless and why load balancing needs it
Choose between layer 4 and layer 7 load balancing, and a balancing algorithm
key_points: Vertical scaling buys a bigger machine and hits a ceiling, and the machine stays a single point of failure; horizontal scaling adds machines behind a load balancer, which works only if servers are stateless, keeping sessions and uploads in shared stores such as a database, Redis or object storage.

A layer 4 load balancer forwards TCP or UDP connections by address and port without reading them; a layer 7 load balancer terminates HTTP (and usually TLS), so it can route by path, header or cookie and retry or rewrite requests, at more cost per request.

Round robin suits identical servers and similar requests; weighted round robin handles servers of different sizes; least connections or least outstanding requests adapt when request costs vary; 'power of two choices' (pick two servers at random, use the less loaded) gets most of the benefit cheaply.

Health checks take failing servers out of rotation: active checks call an endpoint such as /healthz on a schedule, passive checks watch real responses. Keep the check shallow, so one shared dependency's outage doesn't mark every server unhealthy at once.

Don't let the load balancer become the single point of failure: run a redundant pair or a managed service, and spread traffic across instances or regions with DNS or anycast. Drain a server's connections before removing it, so in-flight requests finish.
Sticky sessions pin a user to one server; they make stateful servers work but unbalance the load and lose the sessions when that server dies, so prefer state kept outside the servers.

lessons.title: Timeouts, retries and circuit breakers
objectives: Set a timeout on every remote call
Retry safely with exponential backoff, jitter and a retry budget
Explain how circuit breakers, bulkheads and load shedding contain failures
key_points: Every network call needs a timeout; without one, a slow dependency ties up threads and connections until the caller fails too. Set it from the dependency's measured latency (a little above its p99) and within the whole request's deadline.
Retry only failures that may succeed next time (timeouts, 503 responses, reset connections) and only operations that are safe to repeat; a retried payment needs an idempotency key.

Exponential backoff with jitter spreads retries out, for example a random wait between 0 and min(cap, base × 2^attempt), so thousands of clients don't retry in lockstep and flatten a service that is trying to recover.
Retries multiply load: three attempts at each of three layers can turn one request into 27. Retry at one layer only, and cap retries with a budget, for example at most 10% extra requests.

A circuit breaker counts recent failures; past a threshold it opens and fails calls immediately for a cool-down, then lets a few trial calls through (half-open) and closes if they succeed. The dependency gets room to recover and the caller a fast fallback.

Bulkheads give each dependency its own pool of threads or connections, so a slow one exhausts only its own pool; load shedding rejects excess work early (HTTP 503) instead of queueing it until everything times out.

lessons.title: Rate limiting algorithms
objectives: Compare token bucket, leaky bucket, fixed-window and sliding-window limiters
Decide where to enforce a limit and what to return when it is hit
Explain how to share one limit across many servers
key_points: A token bucket holds up to a capacity of tokens and refills at a steady rate; each request takes a token or is refused. It allows bursts up to the capacity while holding the long-run rate, and stores only two numbers per key: the token count and the time of the last refill.
A leaky bucket queues requests and releases them at a fixed rate, smoothing bursts instead of allowing them; requests that arrive when the queue is full are dropped.

A fixed-window counter (100 a minute, reset on the minute) is simple but lets up to twice the limit through around a window boundary. A sliding-window log stores every request time and is exact but costly; a sliding-window counter weights the previous window's count to approximate it cheaply.
Refuse with HTTP 429 Too Many Requests and a Retry-After header, and limit per API key or user rather than only per IP address, because many users can share one address behind NAT.

Enforce limits at the edge (an API gateway or load balancer) to protect everything behind it, and per service for expensive operations. With many gateway instances, keep counters in a shared store such as Redis and update them atomically.

Decide what happens if the limiter's store is down: failing open keeps the service up but unprotected, failing closed protects it but refuses good traffic. A local, per-instance limit is a common fallback.

import pytest

from ratelimit import FixedWindow, KeyedLimiter, TokenBucket


class FakeClock:
    """A clock the test moves by hand. Times are multiples of 1/8 s, which floats store exactly."""

    def __init__(self, now: float = 0.0):
        self.now = now

    def __call__(self) -> float:
        return self.now

    def advance(self, seconds: float) -> None:
        self.now += seconds


def test_starts_full_and_allows_a_burst():
    bucket = TokenBucket(capacity=5, rate=1, clock=FakeClock())
    assert [bucket.allow() for _ in range(6)] == [True] * 5 + [False]


def test_refills_at_the_rate():
    clock = FakeClock()
    bucket = TokenBucket(capacity=4, rate=4, clock=clock)
    for _ in range(4):
        bucket.allow()
    clock.advance(0.5)                      # 0.5 s x 4 tokens/s = 2 tokens
    assert [bucket.allow() for _ in range(3)] == [True, True, False]


def test_never_holds_more_than_capacity():
    clock = FakeClock()
    bucket = TokenBucket(capacity=3, rate=10, clock=clock)
    clock.advance(100)
    assert sum(bucket.allow() for _ in range(10)) == 3


def test_cost_takes_several_tokens_or_none():
    bucket = TokenBucket(capacity=5, rate=1, clock=FakeClock())
    assert bucket.allow(3) is True
    assert bucket.allow(3) is False         # only 2 left, and a refused request takes nothing
    assert bucket.allow(2) is True


def test_retry_after():
    clock = FakeClock()
    bucket = TokenBucket(capacity=2, rate=4, clock=clock)
    assert bucket.retry_after() == 0
    bucket.allow(2)
    assert bucket.retry_after() == pytest.approx(0.25)
    clock.advance(0.25)
    assert bucket.allow() is True
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        bucket.retry_after(3)


def test_fixed_window_lets_twice_the_limit_through_at_a_boundary():
    clock = FakeClock(0.875)
    window = FixedWindow(limit=10, window=1.0, clock=clock)
    first = sum(window.allow() for _ in range(10))
    clock.advance(0.125)                    # t = 1.0: a new window starts
    second = sum(window.allow() for _ in range(10))
    assert first + second == 20


def test_keyed_limiter_keeps_keys_apart():
    limiter = KeyedLimiter(capacity=2, rate=1, clock=FakeClock())
    assert [limiter.allow("noisy") for _ in range(3)] == [True, True, False]
    assert limiter.allow("quiet") is True
    assert set(limiter.buckets) == {"noisy", "quiet"}

"""Compare a token bucket with a fixed window, then give each user their own bucket."""
import math

from ratelimit import FixedWindow, KeyedLimiter, TokenBucket


class FakeClock:
    def __init__(self, now: float = 0.0):
        self.now = now

    def __call__(self) -> float:
        return self.now


def boundary_burst() -> None:
    """Ten requests just before a window boundary and ten just after it."""
    for name in ("fixed window", "token bucket"):
        clock = FakeClock(0.875)
        limiter = FixedWindow(10, 1.0, clock) if name == "fixed window" else TokenBucket(10, 10, clock)
        allowed = sum(limiter.allow() for _ in range(10))
        clock.now = 1.0
        allowed += sum(limiter.allow() for _ in range(10))
        print(f"Boundary burst of 20 requests in 0.125 s: {name} allowed {allowed}")


def steady_overload() -> None:
    """A client sends 16 requests a second for 4 seconds to a limit of 10 a second, bursts of 10."""
    clock = FakeClock()
    bucket = TokenBucket(capacity=10, rate=10, clock=clock)
    per_second = [0, 0, 0, 0]
    for i in range(64):
        clock.now = i / 16
        if bucket.allow():
            per_second[i // 16] += 1
    print(f"Steady 16 requests/s against 10/s (burst 10): allowed per second {per_second}, "
          f"total {sum(per_second)} of 64")
    wait = bucket.retry_after()
    print(f"Next token in {wait:.4f} s, so the 429 response says Retry-After: {math.ceil(wait)}")


def per_user() -> None:
    """For 2 seconds one user sends 128 requests a second and another 4 a second.
    Each user has their own bucket of 5 tokens, refilling at 5 a second."""
    clock = FakeClock()
    limiter = KeyedLimiter(capacity=5, rate=5, clock=clock)
    sent = {"noisy": 0, "quiet": 0}
    allowed = {"noisy": 0, "quiet": 0}
    for tick in range(256):                 # 2 seconds in steps of 1/128 s, which floats store exactly
        clock.now = tick / 128
        for user in ["noisy"] + (["quiet"] if tick % 32 == 0 else []):
            sent[user] += 1
            allowed[user] += limiter.allow(user)
    for user in ("noisy", "quiet"):
        print(f"User {user}: sent {sent[user]}, allowed {allowed[user]}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    boundary_burst()
    steady_overload()
    per_user()

modules.title: Caching and CDNs
modules.summary: Keep hot data in memory close to where it's needed: choose where caches sit and how they're filled, keep them fresh enough, evict sensibly when they're full, and serve cacheable content from the edge.

lessons.title: Cache-aside and where caches live
objectives: Identify the layers where a system can cache data
Implement the cache-aside read and write paths
Estimate how the hit ratio changes average latency and database load
key_points: Caches sit at every layer: the browser or app, a CDN at the edge, a reverse proxy, an in-process cache in each server, a shared cache such as Redis or Memcached, and the database's own buffer cache. The closer to the user, the faster the hit and the harder the invalidation.

Cache-aside (lazy loading): on a read, look in the cache; on a miss, read the database, store the result with a TTL and return it. The application owns the logic, and the cache holds only data that someone has asked for.

On a write with cache-aside, update the database first and then delete the cached key rather than overwriting it, so the next read loads the current value. Deleting is idempotent and never stores a value computed from stale data.

Average latency = hit ratio × hit latency + (1 − hit ratio) × miss latency. With a 1 ms hit and a 20 ms miss, raising the hit ratio from 90% to 99% cuts the average from 2.9 ms to about 1.2 ms, and cuts database reads tenfold.

A shared cache gives every server the same view and survives server restarts; an in-process cache avoids the network hop but keeps a separate, possibly different, copy in each server, so give it a short TTL.
A cache holds copies, never the only copy: the system must stay correct, if slower, when the cache is empty, restarting or evicting.

lessons.title: Write strategies, invalidation and stampedes
objectives: Compare write-through, write-behind and write-around caching
Choose an invalidation approach and explain the race it must survive
Protect a database from a cache stampede
key_points: Write-through writes to the cache and the database in the same operation, so reads after a write hit and the cache is never behind, at the cost of slower writes and of caching data that may never be read.

Write-behind (write-back) writes to the cache and flushes to the database later in batches: fast writes, but data is lost if the cache fails before the flush, so it suits counters and metrics more than orders. Write-around writes only to the database and lets reads fill the cache.

Ways to invalidate: a TTL bounds staleness even if everything else fails; deleting keys on write keeps data fresh; versioned keys (user:42:v7) make old entries unreachable; change-data-capture events from the database can drive deletes across services.

A classic race: a reader misses and reads the old value, a writer updates the database and deletes the key, then the reader stores the old value, which lasts until its TTL. Short TTLs, version checks or a second, delayed delete limit the damage.

A stampede (thundering herd) happens when a hot key expires and thousands of requests miss at once and hit the database. Let one request recompute while the others wait or get the stale value (request coalescing), refresh hot keys early, and add random jitter to TTLs.

Cache negative results (no such user) briefly, so repeated lookups of missing keys don't all reach the database, and watch for hot keys that overload a single cache node: replicate them or keep them in-process.

lessons.title: Eviction: LRU, LFU and TTL
objectives: Compare LRU, LFU, FIFO and TTL-based expiry
Explain how an LRU cache gets O(1) get and put
Configure a memory limit and eviction policy in Redis
key_points: When a cache is full, its eviction policy decides what to drop. LRU drops the least recently used entry and suits most workloads, where recently used items tend to be used again; LFU drops the least frequently used and protects long-term favourites; FIFO ignores use altogether.

An LRU cache gets O(1) get and put from a hash map (key to node) plus a doubly linked list in order of use: a hit moves its node to the front, an insert adds at the front, and eviction removes from the back. Python's OrderedDict offers both, through move_to_end and popitem(last=False).
One scan of many keys used once can flush an LRU cache of its useful entries. LFU and segmented or two-queue designs resist this, which is why database buffer pools don't use plain LRU.
TTL expiry removes entries by age, whatever their use, and bounds staleness; eviction removes them by need, when memory runs out. Most caches use both.

Redis evicts only once maxmemory is set; maxmemory-policy chooses how, for example allkeys-lru, allkeys-lfu, volatile-lru (only keys with a TTL) or noeviction, which makes writes fail when memory is full. Redis approximates LRU and LFU by sampling keys rather than keeping an exact order.

Size a cache from the working set: when a small share of the keys gets most of the reads, caching that share gives most of the benefit. Measure the hit ratio in production, and grow the cache only while the hit ratio keeps rising.

lessons.title: CDNs and HTTP caching
objectives: Explain how a CDN serves content from edge locations
Control caching with Cache-Control, ETag and versioned file names
Decide what to cache at the edge and how to invalidate it
key_points: A CDN keeps copies of responses at edge locations near users; a request that hits the edge avoids the long round trip to the origin, which serves only the misses. Static assets, images and video are the classic fit, and cacheable API responses can benefit too.

Cache-Control sets the rules: max-age=N lets any cache reuse a response for N seconds, s-maxage overrides it for shared caches such as CDNs, private keeps it to the browser, no-cache allows storing but requires revalidation before each reuse, and no-store forbids storing at all.

Revalidation saves bandwidth: the server sends an ETag (or Last-Modified); later the client sends it back in If-None-Match (or If-Modified-Since), and an unchanged resource gets 304 Not Modified with no body.

Put a version or content hash in static file names (app.3f9a1c.js) and give them a long max-age with immutable: a release changes the name, so nothing needs purging. Keep the HTML short-lived so it picks up the new names.

The cache key is usually the URL; Vary adds request headers to it (Vary: Accept-Encoding keeps compressed and uncompressed copies apart). Never let a shared cache store personalised responses: mark them private or no-store.
Remove edge copies with the CDN's purge API or short TTLs, and use an origin shield (a mid-tier cache) so that a purge or a burst of misses doesn't send every edge location to the origin at once.

"""Serve two files with HTTP caching headers, and answer revalidation with 304 Not Modified."""
import hashlib
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer

APP = b"console.log('app.js, release 1');\n"
FILES = {
    "/app.js": (APP, "public, max-age=60"),                             # a name that never changes
    "/app.3f9a1c.js": (APP, "public, max-age=31536000, immutable"),     # a name that changes per release
}


class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        if self.path not in FILES:
            self.send_error(404)
            return
        body, cache_control = FILES[self.path]
        etag = '"' + hashlib.sha256(body).hexdigest()[:12] + '"'
        if self.headers.get("If-None-Match") == etag:
            self.send_response(304)                      # unchanged: no body
        else:
            self.send_response(200)
            self.send_header("Content-Type", "text/javascript")
            self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(body)))
        self.send_header("Cache-Control", cache_control)
        self.send_header("ETag", etag)
        self.end_headers()
        if self.headers.get("If-None-Match") != etag:
            self.wfile.write(body)


HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 8000), Handler).serve_forever()

from lru import LRUCache


class FakeClock:
    def __init__(self):
        self.now = 0.0

    def __call__(self):
        return self.now


def test_get_and_put():
    cache = LRUCache(2)
    cache.put("a", 1)
    assert cache.get("a") == 1
    assert cache.get("missing", "default") == "default"


def test_evicts_the_least_recently_used():
    cache = LRUCache(2)
    cache.put("a", 1)
    cache.put("b", 2)
    cache.get("a")              # a is now more recent than b
    cache.put("c", 3)           # so b goes
    assert cache.get("b") is None
    assert cache.keys() == ["c", "a"]
    assert cache.evictions == 1


def test_replacing_a_key_refreshes_it_without_growing():
    cache = LRUCache(2)
    cache.put("a", 1)
    cache.put("b", 2)
    cache.put("a", 10)
    assert len(cache) == 2 and cache.keys() == ["a", "b"]
    cache.put("c", 3)
    assert cache.get("a") == 10 and cache.get("b") is None


def test_capacity_one():
    cache = LRUCache(1)
    cache.put("a", 1)
    cache.put("b", 2)
    assert cache.keys() == ["b"]


def test_ttl_expiry_counts_as_a_miss():
    clock = FakeClock()
    cache = LRUCache(10, clock=clock)
    cache.put("session", "xyz", ttl=30)
    clock.now = 29.5
    assert cache.get("session") == "xyz"
    clock.now = 30.0
    assert cache.get("session") is None
    assert len(cache) == 0
    assert (cache.hits, cache.misses) == (1, 1)


def test_delete_is_idempotent():
    cache = LRUCache(2)
    cache.put("a", 1)
    assert cache.delete("a") is True
    assert cache.delete("a") is False
    assert cache.keys() == []


def test_hit_ratio():
    cache = LRUCache(2)
    cache.put("a", 1)
    for key in ["a", "a", "a", "b"]:
        cache.get(key)
    assert cache.hit_ratio == 0.75

"""Cache-aside in front of a slow database: how hit ratio and latency change with cache size,
and why a write should delete the cached copy rather than rely on the TTL alone."""
import random

from lru import LRUCache

HIT_MS, MISS_MS = 1, 20          # a cache read, and a cache miss followed by a database read


def zipf_keys(n_keys: int, n_requests: int, seed: int = 7) -> list[str]:
    """Popularity follows a Zipf-like curve: the key ranked r is requested in proportion to 1/r."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    keys = [f"user:{i}" for i in range(n_keys)]
    weights = [1 / rank for rank in range(1, n_keys + 1)]
    return rng.choices(keys, weights=weights, k=n_requests)


class Database:
    def __init__(self, n_keys: int):
        self.rows = {f"user:{i}": 0 for i in range(n_keys)}   # value = version of the row
        self.reads = 0

    def read(self, key: str) -> int:
        self.reads += 1
        return self.rows[key]


def get_user(cache: LRUCache, db: Database, key: str, ttl: float | None = None) -> tuple[int, int]:
    """Cache-aside read. Returns (value, cost in ms)."""
    value = cache.get(key)
    if value is not None:
        return value, HIT_MS
    value = db.read(key)
    cache.put(key, value, ttl=ttl)
    return value, MISS_MS


def size_experiment() -> None:
    requests = zipf_keys(10_000, 50_000)
    print("Cache-aside, 50,000 reads over 10,000 keys:")
    for capacity in (100, 1_000, 2_000, 5_000):
        cache, db = LRUCache(capacity), Database(10_000)
        cost = sum(get_user(cache, db, key)[1] for key in requests)
        print(f"  capacity {capacity:>5}: hit ratio {cache.hit_ratio:.3f}, database reads {db.reads:>6,}, "
              f"average {cost / len(requests):.2f} ms")


class Clock:
    def __init__(self):
        self.now = 0.0

    def __call__(self) -> float:
        return self.now


def invalidation_experiment() -> None:
    """One operation per 10 ms for 200 s; 2% are writes. Count reads that return an old version."""
    requests = zipf_keys(1_000, 20_000, seed=3)
    for strategy in ("TTL only (60 s)", "delete on write + TTL"):
        rng = random.Random(11)                            # the same writes for both strategies
        clock = Clock()
        cache, db = LRUCache(500, clock=clock), Database(1_000)
        stale = 0
        for i, key in enumerate(requests):
            clock.now = i * 0.01
            if rng.random() < 0.02:                        # a write: update the database first...
                db.rows[key] += 1
                if strategy.startswith("delete"):
                    cache.delete(key)                      # ...then delete the cached copy
            else:
                value, _ = get_user(cache, db, key, ttl=60)
                stale += value != db.rows[key]
        print(f"  {strategy:<22} stale reads: {stale}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    size_experiment()
    print("Invalidation, 20,000 operations, 2% writes:")
    invalidation_experiment()

modules.title: Databases: replication, sharding and consistent hashing
modules.summary: Choose a data store from the access patterns, then scale it: indexes for fast reads, replicas for read capacity and failover, shards for data and write volume, and consistent hashing to place keys. A worked URL shortener puts it together.

lessons.title: SQL or NoSQL, chosen by access pattern
objectives: Compare relational, key-value, document, wide-column and graph databases
Choose a data store from a system's access patterns and consistency needs
Identify the indexes a design's main queries need
key_points: Relational databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL) keep rows in tables with a schema, joins and multi-row ACID transactions. They fit data with relationships and invariants, such as orders, payments and stock, and with indexes and replicas they scale further than is often assumed.

Key-value stores (Redis, DynamoDB) fetch items by key very fast; document stores (MongoDB) keep a whole aggregate, such as a user with their addresses, as one JSON-like document; wide-column stores (Cassandra) partition rows by key for huge, write-heavy, time-ordered data; graph databases answer many-hop questions.

Choose from the access patterns: list the main queries with their rates and latency targets first. Data read together should be stored together, and a store that can't serve the main query by key or index forces full scans or joins in application code.

'NoSQL scales and SQL doesn't' is a myth: what scales is partitioning by a key that spreads the load, which both can do. Many NoSQL stores give up joins, multi-key transactions or ad hoc queries to make partitioning easy.

An index turns a scan of every row into a search of a sorted structure, so give each frequent query an index matching its filter and sort order. Every index also slows writes and takes space, so don't index columns no query uses.
Using several stores is normal: a relational database for orders, Redis for sessions and counters, object storage for images and a search engine for text, each holding the data it serves best.

lessons.title: Replication and read replicas
objectives: Explain leader-follower replication and replication lag
Send reads to replicas without breaking read-your-writes
Describe what can go wrong during failover
key_points: With leader-follower replication, every write goes to the leader, which streams its changes to the followers. Reads can go to followers, which multiplies read capacity and keeps copies ready for failover.

Asynchronous replication keeps writes fast, but followers lag: by milliseconds normally, by seconds or more under load. Synchronous replication to at least one follower means a committed write survives the leader's loss, at the cost of write latency.

Lag breaks read-your-writes: a user saves their profile and the next page, read from a lagging replica, shows the old one. Fixes: read a user's own data from the leader, read from the leader for a short time after a write, or wait until the replica has applied the write's log position.

Failover promotes a follower when the leader dies. With asynchronous replication, writes the old leader hadn't sent are lost, and if it comes back still believing it leads, two leaders (split brain) can accept conflicting writes, so the old leader must be fenced off.
Replicas add read capacity, not write capacity: every write still goes through the leader and is applied on every replica. When writes or data outgrow one leader, the next step is sharding.
Replication isn't a backup: a mistaken DELETE reaches every copy within moments. Keep point-in-time backups as well, and test restoring them.

lessons.title: Sharding and consistent hashing
objectives: Compare range, hash and directory-based sharding
Choose a shard key that spreads load and keeps queries on one shard
Explain how consistent hashing limits data movement when shards change
key_points: Sharding splits data across databases by a shard key, so each shard holds part of the data and takes part of the writes. Range sharding keeps keys in order (good for range scans, prone to hot spots on new keys); hash sharding spreads keys evenly but loses order; a directory maps keys to shards explicitly.

A good shard key has many distinct values, spreads reads and writes evenly, and appears in almost every query, such as a user ID for a user's data. Queries without it must ask every shard (scatter-gather), and transactions across shards need extra machinery.

hash(key) mod N moves almost every key when N changes: going from 4 to 5 shards leaves only about 1 key in 5 where it was. Consistent hashing places shards and keys on a ring and stores each key on the next shard clockwise, so adding a shard moves only about 1/N of the keys, all to the new shard.

Each shard owns many points on the ring (virtual nodes), which evens out the load and lets a bigger machine take more points. With one point per shard, some shards own far more of the ring than others.
Hot keys (a celebrity's profile) can overload one shard under any scheme: cache them, split one logical key over several physical keys with a suffix, or give them dedicated capacity.
Rendezvous (highest random weight) hashing is an alternative: score every node with hash(node, key) and pick the highest. It also moves only the changed node's keys, and needs no ring.

lessons.title: Worked design: a URL shortener
objectives: Estimate the load and storage of a URL shortener
Compare ways to generate short codes
Design a fast, highly available redirect path
key_points: Requirements: create a short code for a long URL, redirect quickly and reliably, and optionally expire links and count clicks. Redirects far outnumber new links (100 to 1 is a common assumption), so the read path drives the design.
Code length follows from the key space: seven base62 characters (a-z, A-Z, 0-9) give 62^7, about 3.5 trillion codes, enough for 100 million new links a day for over 90 years.

Ways to make codes: base62-encoding a unique counter gives short codes without collisions but they're guessable and need ID ranges handed to each server; hashing the URL and keeping 7 characters needs collision checks; random codes checked for uniqueness on insert are simple and hard to guess.
Store code → long URL in a table keyed by the code, which is also a natural shard key, and cache hot codes in Redis or in-process, because a small share of links gets most of the clicks.

301 Moved Permanently lets browsers cache the redirect (fewer requests, but those clicks go uncounted); 302 Found or 307 Temporary Redirect sends every click through the service, so clicks can be counted and the target changed.
Count clicks asynchronously: publish a click event to a queue and aggregate it later, so analytics can never slow down or break a redirect.

from collections import Counter

import base62
from ring import HashRing, modulo_node

IDS = range(1_000_000, 1_100_000)                  # 100,000 links
CODES = [base62.encode(i) for i in IDS]
FOUR = ["db-a", "db-b", "db-c", "db-d"]

print(f"{len(CODES):,} short codes, from {CODES[0]} to {CODES[-1]}")

moved = sum(modulo_node(c, FOUR) != modulo_node(c, FOUR + ["db-e"]) for c in CODES)
print(f"hash mod N, 4 -> 5 shards: {moved / len(CODES):.1%} of keys move")

ring = HashRing(FOUR, vnodes=100)
before = [ring.node_for(c) for c in CODES]
ring.add("db-e")
after = [ring.node_for(c) for c in CODES]
moved = [(b, a) for b, a in zip(before, after) if a != b]
print(f"consistent hashing, 4 -> 5 shards: {len(moved) / len(CODES):.1%} of keys move, "
      f"all of them to {sorted({a for _, a in moved})}")

for vnodes in (1, 10, 100, 1000):
    ring = HashRing([f"db-{i}" for i in range(5)], vnodes=vnodes)
    counts = Counter(ring.node_for(c) for c in CODES)
    mean = len(CODES) / 5
    print(f"vnodes={vnodes:>4}: busiest shard holds {max(counts.values()) / mean:.2f}x the average, "
          f"quietest {min(counts.values()) / mean:.2f}x")

modules.title: Queues, idempotency and worked designs
modules.summary: Move slow work off the request path with queues, make retries and redeliveries safe with idempotency keys and the outbox pattern, and combine everything in two worked designs: a chat service and a news feed.

lessons.title: Message queues and asynchronous processing
objectives: Decide which work belongs off the request path
Compare work queues with publish-subscribe logs
Handle failures with acknowledgements, retries and dead-letter queues
key_points: Move work the user needn't wait for (sending email, resizing images, updating a search index, counting clicks) onto a queue: the request returns once the job is queued, and workers process jobs at their own pace, absorbing bursts.

A work queue (RabbitMQ, Amazon SQS) gives each message to one consumer and removes it once acknowledged; a log (Apache Kafka) keeps messages in ordered, partitioned logs that many consumer groups read independently and can replay.

Order is kept at most within one queue or partition, never globally: send all events for one entity (an order, a conversation) to the same partition by keying on its ID, and accept that different entities interleave.

Delivery is usually at-least-once: a consumer that crashes after doing the work but before acknowledging gets the message again (after a visibility timeout in SQS, or a rebalance in Kafka), so consumers must cope with duplicates.

Retry failed messages with backoff and, after a few attempts, move them to a dead-letter queue for inspection, so one bad message can't block or loop forever. Watch the queue's depth and the age of its oldest message: growth means consumers can't keep up.

Use back-pressure: when consumers fall behind, a bounded queue should push back on producers (refuse, slow them down or shed low-priority work) instead of growing until it runs out of memory or its messages are too old to matter.

lessons.title: Idempotency and safe retries
objectives: Explain why client retries and at-least-once delivery need idempotent operations
Implement idempotency keys for an API
Publish events reliably with the transactional outbox pattern
key_points: An operation is idempotent if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. Setting a status to 'shipped' or deleting a record are naturally idempotent; adding £10 or appending a message are not, and need deduplication.

With idempotency keys, the client makes a unique key (a UUID) for each logical operation and sends it with every retry. The server stores the key, a hash of the request and the response in the same transaction as the effect, replays the stored response for a repeat, and refuses a key reused for a different request.

Make the duplicate check atomic: a UNIQUE constraint on the key, or a single insert-if-absent, stops two concurrent retries from both passing a 'have I seen this?' check. Expire stored keys after a window longer than any client retries for.

Consumers of an at-least-once queue deduplicate the same way: record each processed message ID in the transaction that applies its effect, or make the update conditional, for example applying an event only if its version is newer than the stored one.

Writing to a database and publishing an event touch two systems, so one can succeed without the other. The transactional outbox writes the event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the change, and a relay publishes it afterwards: at least once, with consumers deduplicating.

lessons.title: Worked design: a chat service
objectives: Design real-time message delivery over persistent connections
Order and store messages per conversation
Handle offline users, group chats and presence
key_points: Clients keep a persistent connection (a WebSocket) to a gateway server, and a session service records which gateway each online user is connected to, so a message can be routed to the recipient's gateway and pushed down their connection.

Store a message durably before acknowledging it to the sender, then deliver it. Partition messages by conversation ID and order them by a per-conversation sequence number, which suits a wide-column store and gives every member the same order.
The sender attaches a client-generated message ID, so a retried send isn't stored twice; a client that reconnects asks for every message after the last sequence number it holds.

Offline recipients get a push notification through the platform's service (Apple Push Notification service or Firebase Cloud Messaging) and fetch stored messages when they return; delivery and read receipts are small messages flowing back.

A group message fans out to every member's connection; for big groups, fan out through a queue so the sender doesn't wait for hundreds of deliveries. Presence (online, last seen) comes from heartbeats with a timeout and is cached, because it changes often and needn't be exact.

lessons.title: Worked design: a news feed
objectives: Compare fan-out on write with fan-out on read
Design a hybrid feed that copes with accounts that have millions of followers
Store, cache and paginate feeds
key_points: Fan-out on write (push): when someone posts, add the post's ID to each follower's precomputed feed, so reading a feed is a cheap lookup; but a post from an account with 10 million followers means 10 million writes.

Fan-out on read (pull): build the feed when it's read by fetching recent posts from everyone the user follows and merging them. Posting is cheap, but every feed read is expensive, and feeds are read far more often than posts are written.

The usual answer is a hybrid: push posts from ordinary accounts into followers' feeds and pull posts from the few very large accounts at read time, merging the two; feeds of inactive users can be rebuilt only when they return.

Store each feed as a list of post IDs with a timestamp or score, for example in a Redis sorted set trimmed to the latest few hundred, and fetch the post bodies in one batch from a post cache, so an edited post shows correctly everywhere.

Paginate with a cursor (the score or ID of the last item seen), not an offset, so new posts arriving at the top don't shift the pages and cause duplicates or gaps. Ranking can reorder the candidates once they're gathered.

Run the fan-out asynchronously through a queue: the post request returns once the post is stored, and workers update followers' feeds, so the requirements must accept a short delay before followers see a post.

import sqlite3

import pytest

import payments as p


@pytest.fixture
def conn():
    c = p.connect()
    p.open_account(c, "acct-1", 10_000)
    return c


def test_naive_charge_takes_money_every_time(conn):
    p.naive_charge(conn, "acct-1", 2_500)
    p.naive_charge(conn, "acct-1", 2_500)
    assert p.balance(conn, "acct-1") == 5_000


def test_a_retry_with_the_same_key_charges_once(conn):
    first = p.charge(conn, "acct-1", 2_500, "key-1")
    again = p.charge(conn, "acct-1", 2_500, "key-1")
    assert first == again and first["status"] == "charged"
    assert p.balance(conn, "acct-1") == 7_500
    assert p.charge_count(conn) == 1


def test_different_keys_are_different_payments(conn):
    p.charge(conn, "acct-1", 1_000, "key-1")
    p.charge(conn, "acct-1", 1_000, "key-2")
    assert p.balance(conn, "acct-1") == 8_000


def test_a_reused_key_with_other_parameters_is_rejected(conn):
    p.charge(conn, "acct-1", 1_000, "key-1")
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        p.charge(conn, "acct-1", 9_000, "key-1")
    assert p.balance(conn, "acct-1") == 9_000
    assert not conn.in_transaction


def test_a_decline_is_replayed_too(conn):
    assert p.charge(conn, "acct-1", 50_000, "key-big")["status"] == "declined"
    conn.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance_pence = 100000")
    assert p.charge(conn, "acct-1", 50_000, "key-big")["status"] == "declined"


def test_the_unique_constraint_is_the_real_guard(conn):
    conn.execute("INSERT INTO idempotency_keys VALUES ('k', 'h', '{}')")
    with pytest.raises(sqlite3.IntegrityError):
        conn.execute("INSERT INTO idempotency_keys VALUES ('k', 'h', '{}')")


def test_consumer_skips_redelivered_messages(conn):
    msg = {"id": "m-1", "account_id": "acct-1", "amount_pence": 4_250}
    assert p.handle_order_paid(conn, msg) is True
    assert p.handle_order_paid(conn, msg) is False
    points = conn.execute("SELECT points FROM loyalty_points WHERE account_id = 'acct-1'").fetchone()[0]
    assert points == 42

"""A flaky network loses some requests on the way in and some responses on the way back.
The client can't tell which, so it retries until it gets an answer."""
import random
import uuid

import payments as p


class LostResponse(Exception):
    pass


def flaky(rng: random.Random, call, loss: float = 0.3):
    """Lose the request (the server never sees it) or the response (the server did the work)."""
    if rng.random() < loss / 2:
        raise LostResponse("request lost")
    result = call()
    if rng.random() < loss / 2:
        raise LostResponse("response lost")
    return result


def run(strategy: str, seed: int = 2024) -> None:
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    conn = p.connect()
    p.open_account(conn, "acct-1", 1_000_000)
    attempts = 0
    for _ in range(100):                                    # 100 payments of £5
        key = str(uuid.UUID(int=rng.getrandbits(128), version=4))   # one key per payment, reused by its retries
        while True:
            attempts += 1
            try:
                if strategy == "naive":
                    flaky(rng, lambda: p.naive_charge(conn, "acct-1", 500))
                else:
                    flaky(rng, lambda: p.charge(conn, "acct-1", 500, key))
                break
            except LostResponse:
                continue
    print(f"{strategy}: 100 payments, {attempts} attempts, {p.charge_count(conn)} charges, "
          f"balance {p.balance(conn, 'acct-1'):,} pence")


def redeliveries(seed: int = 7) -> None:
    """At-least-once delivery: a consumer that crashes before acknowledging gets the message again."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    conn = p.connect()
    queue = [{"id": f"order-{i}", "account_id": f"acct-{i % 5}", "amount_pence": 1_000} for i in range(50)]
    deliveries = applied = 0
    while queue:
        msg = queue.pop(0)
        deliveries += 1
        applied += p.handle_order_paid(conn, msg)
        if rng.random() < 0.2:                              # crashed after processing, before the ack
            queue.append(msg)                               # so the broker delivers it again later
    total = conn.execute("SELECT sum(points) FROM loyalty_points").fetchone()[0]
    print(f"queue: 50 messages, {deliveries} deliveries, {applied} applied, {total} points awarded")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run("naive")
    run("idempotent")
    redeliveries()

"""Write updates.csv: ten minutes of courier GPS updates, in the order the service receives them.

Couriers send an update every 4 seconds with a per-courier sequence number. The stream is realistic
rather than clean: about 2% of updates arrive twice (client retries), network delays reorder some
updates, and one courier's app is misconfigured and sends every half second. Same output every run.
"""
import csv
import random

SEED = 314
COURIERS = 200
MINUTES = 10
NORMAL_INTERVAL_MS = 4_000
FAST_COURIER, FAST_INTERVAL_MS = "c-042", 500


def main() -> None:
    rng = random.Random(SEED)
    rows = []
    for c in range(COURIERS):
        courier = f"c-{c:03d}"
        interval = FAST_INTERVAL_MS if courier == FAST_COURIER else NORMAL_INTERVAL_MS
        lat, lon = 13.70 + rng.random() * 0.1, 100.45 + rng.random() * 0.1
        start = rng.randint(0, interval - 1)
        for seq, sent in enumerate(range(start, MINUTES * 60_000, interval), start=1):
            lat += rng.uniform(-0.0004, 0.0004)
            lon += rng.uniform(-0.0004, 0.0004)
            received = sent + rng.randint(40, 400) + (rng.randint(2_000, 9_000) if rng.random() < 0.01 else 0)
            rows.append([received, courier, seq, sent, round(lat, 6), round(lon, 6)])
            if rng.random() < 0.02:                       # a retry: the same update again, a little later
                rows.append([received + rng.randint(500, 3_000), courier, seq, sent, round(lat, 6), round(lon, 6)])
    rows.sort(key=lambda r: (r[0], r[1], r[2]))
    with open("updates.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
        w = csv.writer(f)
        w.writerow(["received_ms", "courier_id", "seq", "sent_ms", "lat", "lon"])
        w.writerows(rows)
    seen, dupes, late, newest = set(), 0, 0, {}
    for _, courier, seq, *_ in rows:
        if (courier, seq) in seen:
            dupes += 1
        elif seq < newest.get(courier, 0):
            late += 1
        seen.add((courier, seq))
        newest[courier] = max(newest.get(courier, 0), seq)
    print(f"Wrote updates.csv: {len(rows):,} rows from {COURIERS} couriers; "
          f"{dupes} duplicates and {late} that arrive after a newer update from the same courier")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
